analogy.p: Think of the outer electron as a dog held on a lead by the nucleus. In lithium the dog is on a short lead, close to the owner, and held firmly. In potassium the lead is long and many people stand in the way, so the dog is held loosely and escapes easily. The easier it escapes, the more reactive the metal. The analogy breaks down because the electron is held by electrical attraction, not a physical lead, and the real attraction depends on both distance and shielding by inner shells.
analogy.t: Holding a pet on a lead

bullets: Group 1 elements are all **metals** found on the **left-hand side** of the periodic table.
Elements in the same group have **similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell**; here that number is **1**.
Electron arrangements: Li **2,1**; Na **2,8,1**; K **2,8,8,1**.
They are **very reactive**, so are **never found uncombined in nature**; they exist in compounds such as sodium chloride.
Because they are so reactive with air and water, they are **stored under oil** (e.g. mineral oil), which keeps oxygen and water vapour away.
Link: the group number tells you the number of outer-shell electrons, so Group 1 atoms form ions with a **1+** charge.
core.h: 1. The alkali metals: position and why they are in Group 1
core.p: The **alkali metals** are the elements in **Group 1** of the periodic table (the first column, on the left): **lithium (Li), sodium (Na), potassium (K), rubidium (Rb), caesium (Cs) and francium (Fr)**. They are called alkali metals because they react with water to form **alkaline** solutions. All have **one electron in their outer shell**, and this single fact explains their properties, their reactions and the trend in reactivity. Hydrogen is placed above Group 1 in many tables but is not an alkali metal.

bullets: **Soft** and easily cut: Li is the hardest of the three, K the softest.
**Low melting points**: Li 181 °C, Na 98 °C, K 63 °C, Rb 39 °C, Cs 29 °C (compare iron at about 1540 °C).
**Low density**: lithium (0.53 g/cm³), sodium (0.97 g/cm³) and potassium (0.86 g/cm³) are less dense than water (1.00 g/cm³), so they **float** on it.
Shiny when freshly cut, then dull as they react with oxygen to form an oxide layer.
**Good conductors** of electricity and heat.
Compared with transition metals: Group 1 metals are **softer, less dense, have lower melting points and are much more reactive**.
core.h: 2. Physical properties of the alkali metals
core.p: The alkali metals are metals, but unusual ones. They are **soft** (they can be cut with a knife), have **low melting and boiling points** and **low density** compared with most metals such as iron or copper. When freshly cut they are **shiny**, but the surface quickly **tarnishes** because the metal reacts with oxygen in the air. Like all metals they are good conductors of heat and electricity because of delocalised electrons in the metallic bonding.

bullets: Trend: melting point **decreases** down the group (Li 181 → Cs 29 °C).
Explanation: **larger atoms** → **weaker metallic bonding** → **less energy** needed to melt.
Each atom contributes **only one** delocalised electron to the 'sea', so the bonding is weak compared with metals such as iron.
Relative atomic mass **increases** down the group (Li 7, Na 23, K 39).
Hardness: metals get **softer** down the group.
Predicting: rubidium has a lower melting point than potassium; caesium would melt in a warm room (melting point about 29 °C).
core.h: 3. Trends in physical properties down the group
core.p: Going down Group 1, the **melting point and boiling point decrease**, the metals get **softer**, and the density generally **increases** (potassium is an exception, being slightly less dense than sodium). The melting point trend is explained by **metallic bonding**: as the atoms get larger, the positive ions are further from the delocalised electrons, so the **attraction (electrostatic forces) between the ions and the delocalised electrons is weaker**, and less energy is needed to overcome it.

bullets: Sodium + chlorine: **2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl** (sodium chloride, white ionic solid).
Lithium + oxygen: **4Li + O₂ → 2Li₂O** (lithium oxide).
Atom to ion: **Na → Na⁺ + e⁻** (the half equation; electrons are lost so this is oxidation).
Sodium ion (2,8) has the same electron arrangement as **neon**; potassium ion (2,8,8) the same as **argon**.
Ionic compounds have **high melting points** and conduct electricity when **molten or dissolved**, not as solids.
Link: formulae use the 1+ charge, e.g. NaCl, K₂O, LiBr (balance the charge).
core.h: 4. Reactions with non-metals: ionic compounds with a 1+ ion
core.p: Group 1 metals **react with non-metals to form ionic compounds**, in which the metal ion carries a **1+ charge**. The metal atom **loses its one outer electron** (this is **oxidation**), forming a positive ion with the electron arrangement of a noble gas (a full outer shell). The non-metal atom gains the electron to form a negative ion. The compounds are typically **white solids that dissolve in water to form colourless solutions**.

bullets: Lithium: **2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂**.
Sodium: **2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂**.
Potassium: **2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂**.
State symbols for Higher: 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g).
Test the solution with **universal indicator**: it turns **purple/blue (pH 13–14)**, showing a strongly alkaline solution.
Test for hydrogen: a **lit splint gives a squeaky pop**.
core.h: 5. Reaction with water: general equation and products
core.p: Group 1 metals **react with water to produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen**. The hydroxide **dissolves in the water to make an alkaline solution** (that is why they are called the alkali metals), and the hydrogen is given off as a gas. The reaction is **exothermic**, releasing heat, which is why the sodium and potassium melt. The general equation is: **metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen**.

bullets: **Lithium**: floats, **fizzes steadily**, moves slowly across the surface, gradually disappears (dissolves); no melting.
**Sodium**: floats, **melts into a ball** (heat released and low melting point), fizzes rapidly, moves quickly, disappears faster.
**Potassium**: floats, melts, moves very quickly, the hydrogen **ignites with a lilac flame**, may spit or explode, and disappears very quickly.
**Rubidium and caesium** (prediction): even more violent, **explode** on contact with water.
Observations that are **evidence of a gas**: fizzing / bubbles; evidence of exothermic reaction: the metal melts, heat produced.
Always write the **order of reactivity: potassium > sodium > lithium**, supported by the speed of the reaction.
core.h: 6. Observations for lithium, sodium and potassium with water
core.p: You must be able to describe what you see for each metal, and you should be able to link the order of reactivity to the observations. All three **float**, **fizz** (hydrogen bubbles) and **move around** on the surface, but the speed of the reaction increases from lithium to potassium. The key observations come from the heat released and the speed.

bullets: Write the logic in order: **more shells → outer electron further from nucleus and more shielding → weaker attraction → electron lost more easily → more reactive**.
Reactivity depends on how easily the atom **loses** an electron, not on how many electrons it has.
The nuclear charge increases down the group, but the extra shells and shielding have a bigger effect, so the attraction to the outer electron is weaker.
Do not write 'the outer electron is easier to take' or 'atoms want to lose electrons more'; use the attraction and distance language.
Contrast with Group 7: halogens must **gain** an electron, which is **harder** when the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so their reactivity **decreases** down the group.
Use the correct words: 'loses its outer electron', 'weaker attraction', 'shielding' (some mark schemes accept 'more shielding').
core.h: 7. Explaining the trend in reactivity (the key 4 to 6 mark answer)
core.p: Reactivity of the alkali metals **increases down the group**. In every reaction the metal atom **loses its outer electron**, so the easier it is to lose, the more reactive the metal. Going down the group, the **atoms get bigger**: the outer electron is in a shell **further from the nucleus**, so the **attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker**; there are also **more inner electron shells shielding** the outer electron from the positive nucleus. Therefore the outer electron is **lost more easily**, and reactivity increases.

bullets: Oxidation half equation: **Na → Na⁺ + e⁻** (OIL: oxidation is loss of electrons).
Reduction half equation (for water): **2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻**.
The **OH⁻ ions** in solution make it alkaline (they raise the pH).
Combine two sodium half equations (2Na → 2Na⁺ + 2e⁻) with the water half equation to get **2Na + 2H₂O → 2Na⁺ + 2OH⁻ + H₂**, i.e. 2NaOH + H₂.
Each sodium atom loses **one** electron; check that electrons lost equals electrons gained.
Link: the reactivity series also relies on how readily metals lose electrons to form positive ions.
core.h: 8. Half equations and redox (Higher tier extension)
core.p: In reactions of alkali metals the metal is **oxidised** (it loses electrons) and the other reactant is **reduced** (it gains them). In the reaction with water, each sodium atom gives up one electron to form Na⁺, and the water gains electrons to form hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions. Writing the half equations shows where the hydroxide comes from and why the solution is alkaline.

bullets: Use a **piece no bigger than a grain of rice** (the amount of hydrogen and heat is then small).
Wear **safety glasses (goggles)** and use a **safety screen**; stand back.
Cut the metal on a tile with a knife; wipe off the **oil** with filter paper; use forceps.
Keep the metal **under oil** in storage; never touch with hands.
Hazards: **corrosive alkali solution**, **flammable hydrogen**, heat from the exothermic reaction, flying hot metal (potassium).
Dispose of residues safely; wash hands; do not let the reaction mixture splash into eyes.
core.h: 9. Safety, handling and the required practical technique
core.p: Alkali metals are hazardous: they react vigorously with water, and the hydroxide solutions formed are **corrosive** (irritant at low concentration); hydrogen is **flammable**. Teacher demonstrations use very small pieces, and the metal is handled with forceps, never fingers (the skin contains water and moisture, causing burns). This is an application of risk assessment skills (working scientifically).

bullets: **Reactivity**: rubidium reacts **more vigorously** than potassium with water (violent or explosive).
**Melting point**: **lower** than potassium (about 39 °C for Rb).
**Hardness**: **softer** than potassium.
**Product with water**: rubidium hydroxide, RbOH, and hydrogen: 2Rb + 2H₂O → 2RbOH + H₂.
**Ion formed**: Rb⁺ (all Group 1 form 1+ ions).
Francium is radioactive and extremely rare, so predictions are rarely tested.
core.h: 10. Predicting properties of rubidium, caesium and francium
core.p: Exam questions often give you data about Li, Na and K and ask for a prediction about Rb or Cs. The skill is to use the **trend** and name it clearly. The predictions must follow the trends in reactivity and melting point.

bullets: Flame colours: **lithium crimson (red)**, **sodium yellow**, **potassium lilac**.
Link to **electrolysis**: sodium and other reactive metals are extracted by electrolysis of molten compounds, not by carbon reduction.
Link to **reactivity series**: potassium, sodium and lithium are at the top, above calcium.
Link to **bonding**: metallic bonding in the metals, ionic bonding in their compounds.
Link to **moles**: the mass of hydrogen from a given mass of metal can be calculated.
Link to **halogens**: Group 1 + Group 7 give salts such as NaCl and KBr.
core.h: 11. Flame tests and links to other topics
core.p: Group 1 metal ions give characteristic **flame test colours**, which links to the analysis topic (flame tests identify metal ions). The alkali metals also link to bonding, electrolysis and the reactivity series. Recognising the connections helps in longer synoptic questions.

bullets: **moles = mass (g) ÷ relative formula mass (Ar or Mr)**.
In 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂, the ratio is 2 mol Na : 1 mol H₂.
**Volume of gas = moles × 24 dm³** (at room temperature and pressure).
**Concentration = moles ÷ volume (dm³)** for the hydroxide solution formed.
Relative atomic masses to use: Li 7, Na 23, K 39, H 1, O 16.
Always show each step, with units, and check the answer is sensible.
core.p: Calculations use the balanced equation to find the amount in moles of a product from the mass of the metal. The method is: **find moles of metal (mass ÷ relative atomic mass), use the mole ratio from the equation, then convert to mass or volume**. For 1 mole of any gas at room temperature and pressure the volume is **24 dm³**.

exam: Name the products: 'metal hydroxide and hydrogen'; write the balanced equation with correct formulae (2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂) for 2 or 3 marks.
'Describe the reaction of potassium with water' (3 marks): floats, melts, moves around, lilac flame, fizzing/bubbles of hydrogen, disappears.
'Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium' (3 to 4 marks): outer electron further from nucleus / more shielding; weaker attraction; electron lost more easily.
In 6-mark questions give a structured answer: electron arrangement (1 outer electron), observations, reaction, equation, trend, explanation.
'Predict' questions: use the trend; say 'more reactive / lower melting point than potassium', and explain.
Use correct terms 'outer electron', 'shell', 'attraction', 'shielding'; avoid 'wants to' or 'pull'.
State test results: indicator turns purple (alkaline), lit splint squeaky pop (hydrogen).
Safety question: say what the hazard is and how to reduce risk (small piece, goggles, safety screen, forceps).
Calculation: show moles, ratio, final value with units (g or dm³).
For data questions quote numbers with units (°C) and describe the trend direction.

mistakes.r: They lose only **one** electron; reactivity increases because the outer electron is **further from the nucleus and more shielded**, so it is lost more easily.
mistakes.w: Reactivity increases because atoms have more electrons to lose.

mistakes.r: Link size to **weaker attraction between nucleus and outer electron**, so it is lost more easily.
mistakes.w: Potassium is more reactive because it is bigger and heavier.

mistakes.r: The products are **sodium hydroxide and hydrogen**: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.
mistakes.w: The products of sodium and water are sodium oxide and hydrogen.

mistakes.r: They form **1+ ions** because they lose one outer electron.
Li, Na and K are less dense than water, so they **float**.
Test for hydrogen is a **lit splint** giving a **squeaky pop**; a glowing splint relights in oxygen.
mistakes.w: Hydrogen is tested with a glowing splint.

mistakes.r: Melting point **decreases** down the group because metallic bonding gets weaker.
mistakes.w: Melting point increases down the group.

mistakes.r: They are stored **under oil** because they react with water and oxygen.
mistakes.w: Alkali metals are kept under water.

mistakes.r: The solution is **alkaline**, universal indicator turns **purple/blue**.
mistakes.w: The solution turns the indicator red because it is acidic.

summary: You must know that Group 1 metals (alkali metals) have one outer electron, form 1+ ions in ionic compounds with non-metals, react with water to give hydrogen and an alkaline metal hydroxide solution, and become more reactive and softer with lower melting points down the group. It matters because it is the key example of explaining a group trend from electron arrangement.

terms.d: The elements in Group 1: lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium.
An electron in the highest occupied energy level; Group 1 atoms have one.
A compound made of oppositely charged ions held by strong electrostatic forces; Group 1 metals form them with non-metals.
A positive ion with a single positive charge formed when an atom loses one electron.
Loss of electrons; Group 1 metals are oxidised when they react.
Gain of electrons; in the reaction with water the hydrogen is reduced.
A compound containing a metal ion and the hydroxide ion OH⁻, e.g. NaOH; alkaline when dissolved.
A solution with pH above 7 containing excess OH⁻ ions; turns universal indicator purple/blue.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, causing a temperature increase.
The reduction of the attraction between the nucleus and outer electron by inner electron shells.
Electrons in metallic bonding that are free to move through the structure.
The electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.
How readily a substance undergoes chemical reactions; for metals, how easily they lose electrons.
A mixture of dyes that changes colour across the pH scale; purple at pH 13–14.
The average mass of atoms of an element compared with one twelfth of a carbon-12 atom.
A test where a metal compound is held in a flame and the colour identifies the metal ion.

worked.ans: Potassium atoms are larger, with the outer electron further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells. The attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker, so the electron is lost more easily and potassium is more reactive.
worked.q: Explain why potassium is more reactive than lithium (4 marks).
steps: Both atoms have one outer electron and react by losing it.
Potassium has more electron shells, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus.
There is more shielding by inner shells, so the attraction to the nucleus is weaker.
So the outer electron is lost more easily.

worked.q: 2.3 g of sodium reacts completely with water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Calculate the volume of hydrogen at room temperature and pressure and the mass of hydrogen. (Ar: Na 23, H 1; 1 mol gas = 24 dm³) (4 marks)
steps: Ratio 2 Na : 1 H₂, so moles H₂ = 0.10 ÷ 2 = 0.050 mol.

worked.ans: Rubidium reacts more violently (explosively) and the hydrogen ignites; equation 2Rb + 2H₂O → 2RbOH + H₂. It is also a softer metal with a lower melting point.
worked.q: Rubidium is below potassium in Group 1. Predict two differences between its reaction with water and that of potassium, and write the equation (3 marks).
steps: Rubidium has its outer electron even further from the nucleus, so it loses it more easily.
Equation: rubidium + water → rubidium hydroxide + hydrogen.
